full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 23.3.88 passed by the learned District Judge, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 67 of 1986 should not be set aside or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The short facts of this matter are that the petitioner being plaintiff instituted Other Suit No. 106 of 1984 in the Court of Munsif, (now Assistant Judge) 2nd Court, Sadar, Chittagong on 15.8.84 for ejectment of the defendant opposite party on the ground of default in payment of rent and of bonafide requirement. The case of the petitioner is that the defendant-opposite party took bhara of the suit premises from the plaintiff as a monthly tenant for serveral years and then executed a bharanama agreement in 1981 and then again renewed the bhara by executing a renewed bharanama agreement on 1.11.83 in favour of the plaintiff. The defendant-opposite party paid rent upto May, 1984 and thereafter stopped payment of rent. The plaintiff-petitioner then served notice upon the defendant-opposite party under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act terminating the monthly tenancy on the expiry of 31st day of July, 1984 and then filed the Other Suit No. 106 of 1984 for ejectment The defendant-opposite party contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the allegations made in the plaint and claiming himself to be a co-sharer in the suit house by purchase from one Halima Khatun and that he filed a partition suit No. 71 of 1985. 

 3. Thereafter when the ejectment suit became ripe for disposal, then the defendant-opposite partyfiled an application under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of learned District Judge, Chittagong being Misc. Case No. 67 of 1986 praying for transfering the Ejectment Suit No. 106 of 1984 from the court of the Assistant Judge to the Court of the 1st Sub-Judge for analogous trial with Partition Suit No. 71 of 1985. The plaintiff- petitioner contested the Transfer Case No. 67 of 1986 by filing a written objection. The learned District Judge after hearing the parties allowed the transfer of the ejectment suit (Other Suit No. 106 of 1984) from the Second Court of Assistant Judge, Chittagong to the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong with a direction for its analogous trial with Partition Suit No. 71 of 1985 vide his judgment and order dated 23.3.88. 

 5. Mr. Md. Ismail, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, submitted that the learned District Judge has committed an error of law and fact by transferring the Ejectment Suit No. 106 of 1984 to the Court of Subordinate Judge for its analogous trial with Partition Suit No. 71 of 1985 in view of the fact that the nature and character of both the suits are quite different from each other and that the laws applicable therein are also different and that the parties of both the suits are not the same. The learned Advocate further argued that the defendant-opposite party is an admitted tenant under the plaintiff- petitioner by executing bharanama agreement and paid rent to him upto May, 1984 and thereafter stopped payment of rent and filed the Partition Suit No. 71 of 1985 and then filed the Transfer Case No. 67 of 1986 with the sole purpose of delaying the disposal of the ejectment suit with the intention of depriving the plaintiff-petitioner from getting his suit house back from the tenant. The learned advocate argued that the defendant-opposite party took bhara of the suit house as a monthly tenant by admitting the plaintiff-petitioner as his landlord by contract and paid rent thereof for a few years and so the opposite party has no right to deny the title of the plaintiff-petitioner. 

 6. In support of his argument, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner referred to a decision in the case of Hajee Abdus Sattar Vs. Mahiuddin & others reported in 38 DLR (AD) 97. It appears that their Lordships have observed in that case the following: 

 "The estoppel as described in this section is known as tenant's estoppel or estoppel by contract. This estoppel is founded upon a contract between the tenant and the landlord. It provides that when a person enters into possession of immovable property as a tenant of another person then neither he nor anybody claiming through him shall be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to deny the landlord's title however defective that title might be. This necessarily implies that in case the tenant sets up a claim of title in himself he shall first surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken it." 

 7. It has been further observed in that case that- "A device resorted to by tenant whereby he defaults to pay rent and when sued for evictien, sets up plea of no relationship of tenant and landlord such a plea is unavailing when original of tenancy is proved." 

 8. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner next referred to the case of Abdul Jahar Vs. Abdul Kader & others reported in 36 DLR 306 and said that in that case their Lordships have observed the following: 

 10. Mr. Md. Nurul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the defendant-opposite party argued that the learned District Judge has wide power of transferring any suit from one court to another and, as such, the learned District Judge, Chittagong has not committed any error of law in transferring the Ejectment Suit-No. 106 of 1984 from the Court of Assistant Judge to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong. The learned Advocate further argued that in deciding this revisional application the only question to be considered is whether the learned District Judge has committed any error of law occasioning failure of justice, but that the facts of the case are not matters for consideration in this revisional application. 

 11. It is true that the facts of the case are not necessarily to be considered in deciding whether an order of transfer under section 24 of the Code of Civil Procedure has become legal or there has been any error of law in passing that order, But in deciding such a question in respect of an order of transfer of a case on the sole ground of an analogous trial with another case, it needs to be seen whether the facts and nature of the cases are conducive for such transfer on the sole ground of an analogous trial of both the cases. 

 14. It is argued on behalf of the defendant-opposite party that the District Judge has wide power of transfer of any case at any stage from one court to another for convenience and inconvenience of the parties. It is true that the District Judge has got such wide power of transferring a suit. But it is a settled principle of law as cited above that the convenience of transfer which is to be taken into consideration by the court is the convenience of both the parties, not only one of them. From the circumstances of the matter, it will appear that the impugned order of transfer as made by the learned District Judge will be convenient to serve the purpose of the defendant-opposite party to delay the disposal of the ejectment suit but it will be most inconvenient and prejudicial to the interest of the plaintiff-petitioner. 

 15. Mr. Md. Ismail, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner next argued that the guiding principle of analogous trial of two suits are that the nature and character of both the suits must be same or similar, the parties must be more or less same and same set of witnesses will be there in both the suits on behalf of both parties and issues will be almost same in both the suits, but that none of these guiding factors are present in the ejectment suit and the partition suit. The learned Advocate further argued that the District Judge cannot also direct the transferee court for analogous trial of any transferred suit with another suit. In this connection, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner referred to the case of Dronavaijuls Vidyamba Vs. Vallabhajosyulla Lakshmi Venkayamma reported in AIR (Andhra Pradesh) 1958 page 218 wherein it has been held that "For whatever reasons of convenience or otherwise the order of transfer is made under section 24(2) CPC, it does not empower the court or contemplate any directions being given for the joint trial of the transferred suit." 

 18. For all the reasons stated above, I am of the opinion that this is a fit case for interference by this court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
